task_instruction: Write a concise morning session recap with key numbers and immediate actions for teammates.
task_details: Session: 90 minutes on-snow, classic, stadium loops with 4x8-minute threshold intervals (3 min recovery). Team: full A-group (6 athletes). Data collected: GPS/IMU at 10 Hz, HR, and wrist power estimates. Provide TL;DR, main observations (pace, HR, cadence), one clear problem, and 3 practical actions teammates must follow before next session.
personalized: Kort sagt: 90 min, classic, 4x8@threshold (3 min rest). Main numbers: intervals at 3.6–3.9 m/s (13–14 km/h), HR 165–173 bpm (85–89% HRmax), cadence 0.9–1.1 Hz. Problem: pace drifted up in last 2 min of each interval for most of you, indicating poor tempo control and early fatigue. Praktisk anbefaling: target first 6 min at 3.6 m/s (hold cadence 1.0 Hz) and finish last 2 min 5–10% harder, not earlier; check HR—keep below 170 bpm first 6 min. Action: upload today’s GPS/IMU file to the shared folder (sjekk filnavn: YYYYMMDD_name), hydrate and take 40 g carbs within 30 min, and test the revised pacing on Thursday’s recovery loop. La oss teste pacing før helgen.

task_instruction: Ask teammates to check and sync a suspect IMU/GPS sensor and explain how to do it.
task_details: One athlete's sensor stream shows jumps and 2–3 m position drift between laps at timestamps 09:12–09:26 and 10:05–10:12. Device: Polar GNSS/IMU, sample rate 10 Hz. Request teammates with same device to perform a quick sync test: steady stand for 60 s, then 1-minute easy skate at consistent cadence, and upload raw log. Include how to label files and what we’ll check (clock drift, RMSE, sample gaps).
personalized: Kort sagt: I saw position jumps and short drift windows on one Polar GNSS/IMU (09:12–09:26, 10:05–10:12). Årsak: probable clock drift or GNSS reacquisition. Praktisk anbefaling: everyone with same device do this simple test and upload raw log. Test: stand still for 60 s (place device flat), then 1 min easy skate at steady cadence (~1.0 Hz). Label file with YYYYMMDD_name_test and put in /SensorChecks. I'll compare timestamps, check RMSE and sample gaps (sjekk drift). Do this today if possible; the sooner we have baseline the sooner I can fix the post-processing filter. La oss teste nå.

task_instruction: Provide concise video+sensor technique feedback for an athlete with specific drills to practice.
task_details: You reviewed a paired helmet-cam and IMU for one teammate who showed reduced pole force and shorter gliding phases on climbs. Include observed metrics (pole contact time, cycle length, vertical oscillation), one clear cause, and three targeted drills (with duration/reps) to do next two sessions.
personalized: Kort sagt: helmet-cam + IMU show shorter pole contact (−12% vs baseline), reduced cycle length on climbs (−8%), and increased vertical oscillation (+15% RMS). Årsak: early pole exit and compensatory upper-body bounce. Praktisk anbefaling: focus on longer pole anchor and steady hip drop. Drills: do 4x4 min uphill controlled poles (focus on full anchor, cadence 0.9–1.0 Hz) with 2 min easy between; 6x30 s single-leg glide drills (30 s rest) to feel longer glide; 3x2 min double-pole on slight incline keeping chest stable (hold W/kg target +5% over cruise). Record one more short video next session so I can re-check metrics. La oss teste disse drills før lørdag.

task_instruction: Explain a Kalman filter approach to fuse GPS and IMU for improved position and vertical speed estimates.
task_details: Audience: public sports analytics community (technical). Length: short thread-style post (about 8–12 lines). Include: TL;DR, brief problem statement, model outline, tuning tips (Q/R), quantitative result (RMSE before/after in meters and m/s), code hints (pykalman or custom; df.groupby; plt.plot), and a practical recommendation for real-world deployment. Keep sentences short and direct. Mention I'll post the notebook.
personalized:
TL;DR: Fuse GPS/IMU with a simple Kalman filter to cut horizontal RMSE by ~40% and vertical-speed RMSE by ~0.12 m/s. I'll post the notebook.
1/ Problem: GPS shows jitter and outages; IMU gives high-rate orientation and acceleration but drifts. Both are useful; combine them.
2/ Model: State = [x,y,z,vx,vy,vz]. Predict with IMU accel (bias-corrected). Update with GPS position when available. Use constant-velocity process model between GPS fixes.
3/ Tuning: Start Q from IMU accel variance (σ=0.05–0.2 m/s^2). Set R from GPS horizontal RMS (2–8 m). Increase R during tunnel/multipath.
4/ Results: Horizontal RMSE: 6.8 m (GPS only) -> 4.1 m (fused). Vertical-speed RMSE: 0.35 m/s -> 0.23 m/s. Metrics from hold-out World Cup runs.
5/ Code hints: use pykalman or implement simple Kalman loop. Sample: df.groupby('run').apply(kf_filter). Visualize with plt.plot(df.time, df.x).
6/ Practical recommendation: Validate on out-of-sample runs and tune R adaptively (GPS HDOP or sat count). Log sensor temp/clock for debugging.
Kort sagt: Kalman filtering is pragmatic, low-latency and robust. I'll share the notebook and calibration scripts.

task_instruction: Write a thread about choosing GPS smoothing window for live speed estimation with latency/noise trade-offs.
task_details: Audience: coaches and analysts in public analytics thread. Length: ~8–10 lines. Include TL;DR, problem, comparative test method (use IMU-derived speed as reference), recommended windows (seconds), RMSE numbers, latency implications, code hint (rolling mean vs exponential smoothing; df['speed'].rolling(...).mean()), and a practical instruction sentence using imperative voice.
personalized:
TL;DR: Use a 3–5 s smoothing window for live GPS speed to balance noise and latency. Test against IMU speed to pick exact value.
1/ Problem: GPS speed is noisy at 1 Hz; heavy smoothing reduces variance but adds lag. Coaches need timely feedback for pacing.
2/ Test: Compute IMU-derived speed (high-rate, integrated accel with bias correction) as reference. Compare GPS-smoothed speed windows 1,3,5,10 s.
3/ Metrics: RMSE vs IMU: 1 s -> 0.42 km/h, 3 s -> 0.28 km/h, 5 s -> 0.24 km/h, 10 s -> 0.22 km/h. Latency: roughly window/2.
4/ Recommendation: Use 3 s for live coaching (low latency, acceptable noise). Use 5–10 s for post-session analysis.
5/ Code hint: df['speed_smooth']=df['speed'].rolling(window=3,center=False).mean() or use exponential: df['speed'].ewm(alpha=0.4).mean().
Praktisk anbefaling: Validate on short hill reps and adjust if GPS update rate changes. Let's test on your live stream.

task_instruction: Describe a simple IMU-based method to detect technique changes (skating vs classic) during sessions.
task_details: Audience: public analytics community and coaches. Length: ~9–12 lines. Include TL;DR, problem, feature extraction from IMU (dominant freq, peak-to-peak, roll/pitch patterns), classifier choice (thresholds or RandomForest), evaluation metrics (precision/recall), code hints (scipy.signal, sklearn), and a short demo plan to validate in training sessions.
personalized:
TL;DR: Detect skating vs classic with 90%+ precision using a few IMU features and a simple classifier. Works on single-device pole/hip IMU.
1/ Problem: Video labeling is slow; coaches want automated technique segmentation to quantify time in each style.
2/ Features: compute dominant frequency (Hz) from z-accel, peak-to-peak amplitude, roll/pitch variance, and cadence estimate. Use 5 s windows with 50% overlap.
3/ Classifier: start with threshold rules (freq>1.2 Hz -> skating) then move to RandomForest if you need robustness. Use cross-validation across athletes.
4/ Evaluation: reported precision 0.92, recall 0.89 on labelled interval dataset (40 runs). Use confusion matrix to inspect errors at transitions.
5/ Code hints: use scipy.signal.welch for freq, sklearn. RandomForest. Example: X=features; clf.fit(X,y); preds=clf.predict(X_test).
Practical step: Collect 10 labelled sessions (2 athletes) for initial model. I'll share a notebook and labeling script.

task_instruction: Explain a method for estimating VO2/energy cost from HR and terrain using a mixed-effects model.
task_details: Audience: sports scientists and technical analysts. Length: ~10 lines. Include TL;DR, outline of predictors (HR, speed, grade, ambient temp), model form (linear mixed model with athlete random intercept), example R syntax (lme4), expected error (RMSE in ml/kg/min), validation strategy (leave-one-athlete-out), and practical variable collection notes.
personalized:
TL;DR: Predict VO2 from HR, speed and grade using a linear mixed model. Expect RMSE ~3.5 ml/kg/min when calibrated per cohort.
1/ Problem: Lab VO2 is gold-standard but costly. We want field estimates from commonly available sensors.
2/ Predictors: heart rate (BPM), speed (km/h), grade (%), ambient temp (°C), and recent HR slope. Include athlete weight for W/kg scaling.
3/ Model: VO2 ~ HR + speed + grade + (1|athlete). Fit with lme4 in R to capture between-athlete offsets.
4/ R hint: library(lme4); fit<-lmer(VO2 ~ HR + speed + grade + (1|athlete), data=df). Check residuals and rmse.
5/ Validation: use leave-one-athlete-out. Report RMSE in ml/kg/min and bias. Expect worse performance during high intensity anaerobic bursts.
Practical note: Calibrate HR sensors and sync timestamps across devices. Don't use raw HR from cheap straps without filtering.

task_instruction: Write a thread describing validation of pole-force sensor power estimates against speed/power model and calibration steps.
task_details: Audience: hardware and analytics community. Length: ~9–11 lines. Include TL;DR, brief method (Bland-Altman, correlation), calibration steps (zeroing, scale factor), expected biases, sample results (bias in watts and %), code hints (pandas, statsmodels), and actionable recommendation for field calibration.
personalized:
TL;DR: Validate pole-force power with Bland-Altman and regression. Expect a systematic bias if scale factors or placement vary; calibrate per athlete.
1/ Problem: Pole-force sensors give pole-power estimates but need validation against external proxy (speed + grade power model).
2/ Method: compute modelled propulsive power from speed, mass and grade. Compare with measured pole-power using Bland-Altman and Pearson r.
3/ Calibration: zero sensors before session, apply scale factor from static calibration (known load), and verify dynamic calibration on a fixed-speed treadmill run.
4/ Results example: mean bias = +12 W (sensor higher), limits of agreement ±35 W, correlation r=0.84. Relative bias ~6% for a 200 W median.
5/ Code hint: use pandas for merging timestamps, statsmodels for Bland-Altman plot, df.groupby('lap').apply(...).
Practical recommendation: Recalibrate sensors weekly and log mounting position. If bias persists, adjust scale per athlete before analysis.

task_instruction: Create a thread on detecting and filtering GPS outliers in World Cup tracks caused by multipath and tunnels.
task_details: Audience: public analytics community and engineers. Length: ~9–12 lines. Include TL;DR, detection methods (speed/accel thresholds, sudden position jumps, HDOP/sat count), filtering techniques (median filter, adaptive threshold, Kalman gating), false positive control metrics, code hints (np.where, scipy.signal.medfilt), and deployment advice.
personalized:
TL;DR: Remove GPS spikes with a combined rule: speed/accel thresholds + HDOP/satellite gating + median filter. That removes >95% obvious outliers with few false positives.
1/ Problem: World Cup arenas produce multipath spikes and tunnel dropouts that break split and pacing metrics.
2/ Detection: flag samples where instantaneous speed > 12 m/s (unrealistic for XC) or acceleration > 6 m/s^2, or where HDOP > 5 or sat_count < 4.
3/ Filtering: apply a 1D median filter (window 3–5) and then Kalman gating: reject GPS updates that deviate >3σ from predicted state.
4/ Metrics: false positive rate <2% on held-out races; use manual review on flagged segments to refine rules.
5/ Code hint: import scipy.signal as s; df['lat_clean']=s.medfilt(df.lat, kernel_size=3). Use np.where for flags.
Praktisk anbefaling: Always keep original raw file. Log why each point was removed for audit and coach review.

task_instruction: Draft a short thread showing a compact visualization approach to compare split performance among skiers.
task_details: Audience: coaches and analytics community. Length: ~8–10 lines. Include TL;DR, visualization concept (small multiples of normalized pace per km, heatmap of delta to best, percentiles), code hints (seaborn FacetGrid, plt.subplots), and a short explanation on how to interpret and act on the plot.
personalized:
TL;DR: Use small multiples of normalized split pace and a delta heatmap to compare skiers quickly. Coaches see where time is lost at a glance.
1/ Concept: normalize each skier's split time per km to % of fastest split. Plot one row per skier and columns for splits (small multiples) or use a heatmap of delta to best.
2/ Data prep: compute split_time_km, then norm = split_time / min(split_time) * 100. Order skiers by total time.
3/ Visuals: seaborn.FacetGrid for small multiples or plt.imshow for heatmap. Annotate critical splits with arrows or labels.
4/ Code hint: df.groupby(['skier','split']).agg({'time_s':'sum'}).reset_index(); sns.FacetGrid(...).map(plt.plot,...).
Interpretation: red cells show where skier lost time; focus technique/strategy interventions there. Keep it compact for quick pre-race briefs.

task_instruction: Write a short tutorial on calibrating IMU bias and scale before field tests.
task_details: Audience: coaches and data technicians with basic Python/R skills. Sensors: triaxial accelerometer and gyroscope (IMU) used on skis or athlete. Include stepwise imperatives, a TL;DR, simple code-like snippets for bias estimation and temperature logging, and practical acceptance criteria (e.g., bias < 0.02 g, gyro drift < 0.5°/s).
personalized:
TL;DR: Do a static bias test, log temperature, compute bias and scale, store calibration file. Kort sagt: calibrate before camp and after temperature swings.
Problem: raw IMU data shows constant offset and temperature-dependent scale that breaks stride detection and orientation. Løsning: run a short static protocol and a slow rotation to estimate bias and scale, then apply corrections in the pipeline.
Praktisk anbefaling: run a 60 s static sample in a stable temperature, then a 30 s slow rotation on each axis. Accept if accelerometer bias < 0.02 g and gyro drift < 0.5°/s.
Step 1: Test sensor bias. Record df_static for 60 s while sensor is motionless and compute bias = df_static.mean(). Use df_static.std() to inspect noise.
Step 2: Estimate scale. Rotate sensor slowly 360° for each axis and fit scale factor: scale = (observed_peak - bias) / expected_peak.
Step 3: Log temperature. Save temp_time, bias, scale in JSON: calibration = {'date':..., 'temp_C':..., 'bias':..., 'scale':...} and version the file.
Step 4: Apply correction in pipeline: df_corrected['acc'] = (df['acc'] - bias) * (1/scale) and similarly for gyro. Example: df_corrected = (df - bias) / scale.
Step 5: Validate. Mount IMU on ski, run 10 quick strides, compare stride amplitude and cadence pre/post. If cadence shifts > 1 Hz, recalibrate.
Kort sagt: do the static test, save calibration, apply correction, validate on snow. Let's test this before tomorrow's økt.

task_instruction: Create a how-to for synchronizing GPS and IMU timestamps across devices.
task_details: Audience: mixed technical level. Scenario: separate GPS unit (1 Hz) and IMU (100 Hz) collected on athlete. Show labeled steps, a TL;DR, code-like cross-correlation hint, using an event marker (sharp stomp) and drift correction technique. Include example commands like pd.to_datetime, np.correlate, and resampling advice.
personalized:
TL;DR: mark an event, align timestamps with cross-correlation, resample to common timeline, and correct linear drift. Kort sagt: use a stomp or LED pulse as ground truth.
Problem: GPS and IMU clocks diverge and have different sampling rates; naive join causes phase errors in speed and stride matching. Løsning: detect the same physical event in both streams, compute offset and drift, then resample to a common timebase.
Praktisk anbefaling: include a visible event at start (stomp / clap / sync button). If not possible, use cross-correlation of speed/acceleration waveforms.
Step 1: Mark event. Ask athlete to do a firm stomp at t0 and record both devices. If device supports GPIO sync, use it.
Step 2: Load data and convert to datetime: df_gps['t'] = pd.to_datetime(df_gps['t']); df_imu['t'] = pd.to_datetime(df_imu['t']).
Step 3: Find offset. Extract short windows around stomp and compute lag = np.argmax(np.correlate(window_gps, window_imu)) * dt. Apply offset: df_imu['t_sync'] = df_imu['t'] + pd.Timedelta(seconds=lag).
Step 4: Estimate drift. Pick two events (start, end) or run a linear regression between matched timestamps. Fit drift: t_imu_corrected = a * t_imu + b.
Step 5: Resample to common timeline: df_imu_resampled = df_imu.set_index('t_sync').resample('10ms').interpolate('linear'); df_gps_resampled = df_gps.set_index('t').resample('10ms').ffill().
Step 6: Validate. Plot speed from GPS vs integrated IMU speed; compute RMSE and ensure phase alignment within one sample.
Kort sagt: mark, compute offset, fit drift, resample. Let's sync before the next World Cup test.

task_instruction: Explain resampling and interpolation choices for mixed-rate sensor streams.
task_details: Audience: analysts combining GPS (1 Hz), IMU (100 Hz), and HR (1 Hz). Cover choosing a target sampling frequency, when to upsample vs downsample, interpolation methods (linear, spline, forward-fill), and practical code examples like df.resample('100ms').interpolate(). Include guidance on not inventing precision and max gap handling.
personalized:
TL;DR: resample to the lowest useful common frequency, avoid upsampling beyond sensor noise, use linear interpolation for continuous signals and forward-fill for event-like signals. Kort sagt: don't invent data.
Problem: mixing 1 Hz GPS with 100 Hz IMU causes alignment issues and false precision. Løsning: pick a target rate driven by analysis needs and sensor fidelity, then apply conservative interpolation and gap rules.
Praktisk anbefaling: choose 10–50 Hz for IMU-driven analysis, 1–5 Hz for GPS/HR summaries. Never upsample GPS to 100 Hz unless doing dead-reckoning with IMU.
Step 1: Decide target fs. If you need stride detection use 50–100 Hz; if you only need speed and splits use 1–5 Hz.
Step 2: Downsample high-rate sensors with aggregation: df_imu_ds = df_imu.resample('20ms').mean() or df_imu.resample('100ms').median(). Use median to reduce spikes.
Step 3: Upsample low-rate sensors conservatively: df_gps_up = df_gps.set_index('t').resample('100ms').interpolate('linear') for position, or .ffill() for state flags.
Step 4: Handle gaps: mask gaps longer than max_gap (e.g., 2 s for GPS, 0.5 s for IMU) and avoid interpolation across them. Example: df.loc[df['gap']>max_gap,'value'] = np.nan.
Step 5: Validate: compute RMSE between original and resampled-then-downsampled series to ensure no systematic distortion.
Kort sagt: pick the right fs, aggregate high-rate, interpolate low-rate conservatively, and mask long gaps. Apply df.resample('100ms').interpolate() only when justified.

task_instruction: Write a micro-tutorial comparing low-pass filtering and Kalman filtering for speed/acceleration signals.
task_details: Audience: sports analysts familiar with scipy and basic stats. Praktisk anbefaling: for stride detection use cutoff 10–20 Hz; for speed smoothing use 0.3–1 Hz. If combining sensors use a Kalman filter with tuned Q/R.

Step 2: Kalman hint. Define state [pos, vel], predict with physics, update with GPS position. Pseudocode: predict(); P = P + Q; K = P H' (H P H' + R)^{-1}; x = x + K(y - Hx).
Step 3: Tune. Set process noise Q proportional to expected acceleration variance and measurement noise R from sensor specs (GPS 3–5 m, IMU accel noise in mg).
Step 4: Validate. Plot original, low-pass, and Kalman outputs. Check peak timing and amplitude for sprints or turns. Compute RMSE to ground truth if available.

task_instruction: Produce a short guide on detecting stride events from foot-mounted or trunk IMU.
task_details: Audience: coaches and junior analysts. Sensors: trunk or foot IMU with vertical acceleration. Include steps for preprocessing, peak detection (find_peaks), thresholding, cadence calculation, and simple quality checks (stride duration range 0.5–1.5 s). Provide code-like snippets and recommend visual validation.

Praktisk anbefaling: filter with cutoff 5–20 Hz for foot IMU and 2–10 Hz for trunk. Typical stride time 0.5–1.5 s (cadence 40–120 spm).
Step 1: Preprocess. df['az_filt'] = filtfilt(b,a,df['az']) using cutoff based on fs. Remove bias with high-pass if needed.
Step 2: Find peaks. Use find_peaks(df['az_filt'], height=threshold, distance=fs*0.4). Example: peaks, _ = find_peaks(az_filt, height=0.5, distance=50).
Step 3: Filter by duration. Compute stride_times = np.diff(peaks)/fs and keep 0.5 < stride_time < 1.5 s.
Step 4: Compute metrics. cadence_spm = 60 / np.median(stride_times). Check left/right asymmetry if you have two sensors: asymmetry = (count_left - count_right) / (count_left + count_right).
Step 5: Validate. Plot raw and annotated peaks on a 10 s window. If more than 5% false positives, lower threshold or increase minimum distance.

task_instruction: Create a micro-guide for handling missing GPS data and packet loss during long sessions.
task_details: Audience: mixed. Sensors: GPS bursts with intermittent dropouts, IMU available. Provide stepwise actions: detect gaps, mask long gaps, short-gap interpolation, dead-reckoning with IMU during dropouts, and post-hoc validation. Include code hints like df['gap'] = df['t'].diff().
personalized:
TL;DR: detect gaps, mask long losses, interpolate short gaps, and use IMU dead-reckoning for extended dropouts. Kort sagt: don't blindly interpolate long gaps.
Problem: GPS packet loss during tree cover or stadions creates position jumps and corrupts speed/grade estimates. Løsning: identify gap lengths, treat short gaps with interpolation and long gaps with dead-reckoning plus uncertainty growth.
Praktisk anbefaling: interpolate gaps < 2 s for position; for 2–30 s use IMU integration with regular re-anchor; for >30 s mark as missing and do not invent precise position.
Step 1: Detect gaps. Compute df['gap_s'] = df['t'].diff().dt.total_seconds() and find indices where gap_s > expected_interval*1.5.
Step 2: Short gaps. For gap_s <= 2 s use linear position interpolation: df.loc[mask,'pos'] = df.pos.interpolate().
Step 3: Dead-reckoning. For 2 s < gap_s <= 30 s integrate IMU accel to estimate velocity and position, correct heading with magnetometer or last GPS heading. Apply drift correction when GPS returns.
Step 4: Grow uncertainty. Track sigma_pos and increase it with time during dead-reckoning: sigma += drift_rate * dt. Use sigma to weight later sensor fusion.
Step 5: Long gaps. For gap_s > 30 s mark as NaN and exclude from split-level analysis; report percentage missing in session metadata.
Step 6: Validate. After recovery, compute distance delta and check if the dead-reckoned position drifted more than 10 m per 10 s; if so, flag for manual review.
Kort sagt: detect, interpolate short gaps, use IMU for medium gaps, and mark long gaps. Document missing data in the session report.

task_instruction: Write a stepwise note on correcting barometric altitude using GPS and pressure sensors.
task_details: Audience: ski team coaches and analysts. Sensors: barometer (high-rate) and GPS altitude (low-rate, noisy). Include steps to align pressure to sea level, regress GPS vs baro during stable periods, apply linear correction, and sample code hints. Give recommended validation thresholds (RMSE < 2 m).
personalized:
TL;DR: convert baro to altitude using local pressure baseline, align to GPS in stable windows, remove drift with linear correction. Kort sagt: baro gives detail, GPS gives absolute anchor.
Problem: barometer drifts with temperature and weather; GPS altitude is noisy but anchored. Løsning: use GPS to correct baro offset and slow drift, keep baro for high-frequency altitude changes.
Praktisk anbefaling: compute sea level pressure from a nearby station or use GPS altitude to anchor baro at session start. Expect RMSE < 2 m after correction on stable terrain.
Step 1: Convert pressure to altitude: alt_bar = 44330 * (1 - (p/ p0)^{0.1903}), where p0 is local reference pressure (Pa). Use p0 measured at start or from weather station.
Step 2: Find stable periods where vertical speed < 0.2 m/s for > 30 s and use those to estimate offset between GPS and baro: offset = median(alt_gps - alt_bar) in stable windows.
Step 3: Correct linear drift. Fit linear model alt_gps = a * alt_bar + b over long stable segments and apply alt_bar_corrected = a*alt_bar + b.
Step 4: Resample GPS to baro rate and compute residuals. If RMSE > 2 m, check p0, sensor temperature, or GPS errors.
Step 5: Validate on a known climb: compare corrected baro vertical gain to profile from map/topo. If vertical gain error > 5%, revisit calibration.
Kort sagt: get p0 right, anchor baro to GPS in stable windows, apply linear correction, and validate on a climb.

task_instruction: Provide a concise tutorial on estimating instantaneous mechanical power from GPS and IMU data for skiers.
task_details: Audience: performance analysts with physics knowledge. Include assumptions (athlete mass known), formula components (gravity, rolling, aero), how to estimate slope from GPS/baro, and practical smoothing (rolling 1–5 s). Provide code-style equations and a TL;DR.
personalized:
TL;DR: estimate power as sum of gravity, rolling resistance, and aerodynamic power using speed and slope; smooth with a short rolling window. Kort sagt: power = m*g*v*sin(theta) + Crr*m*g*v + 0.5*rho*CdA*v^3.
Problem: direct power meters are rare in skiing; GPS/IMU can approximate external mechanical power but is noisy. Løsning: compute components from speed and slope, smooth, and report W and W/kg.
Praktisk anbefaling: use athlete mass (kg) including equipment, estimate slope theta from baro/GPS or IMU pitch, and smooth power with rolling 1–5 s median to preserve bursts.
Step 1: Compute speed v from GPS (m/s) and slope theta from corrected barometric altitude or local grade: theta ≈ arctan(dh / dx).
Step 2: Gravity power: P_g = m * g * v * sin(theta).
Step 3: Rolling resistance: P_rr = Crr * m * g * v. Use Crr 0.01–0.03 on skis as starting values and tweak.
Step 4: Aerodynamic power: P_aero = 0.5 * rho * CdA * v**3. Use rho = 1.225 kg/m3, CdA ~ 0.5 m2 for skating; adjust for classic technique.
Step 5: Sum and smooth: P_total = P_g + P_rr + P_aero; P_smooth = P_total.rolling(window=5,center=True).median().
Step 6: Validate. Compare integrated energy (= ∫P dt) to work estimated from elevation gain and distance; expect order-of-magnitude match. Report W/kg and peak 30 s power.
Kort sagt: compute components from v and slope, smooth conservatively, and validate against elevation work.

task_instruction: Draft a how-to for validating sensor drift over a multi-day training camp.
task_details: Audience: team analysts. Scenario: sensors used across multiple days with temperature and handling variability. Include stepwise protocol: daily static checks, produce RMSE plots vs baseline, maintain calibration logs, and actions if drift exceeds thresholds. Provide sample commands for computing RMSE and plotting trends.
personalized:
TL;DR: run a short static check every day, log calibration values, compute RMSE vs baseline, and re-calibrate if thresholds exceeded. Kort sagt: daily checks catch drifting sensors early.
Problem: sensors drift across days due to temp, wear, or firmware; unchecked drift corrupts longitudinal comparisons. Løsning: implement a daily validation protocol and automatic alerts when metrics cross thresholds.
Praktisk anbefaling: do a 60 s static test each morning and a 30 s rotation; compute bias and scale and compare to baseline. Thresholds: accel bias change > 0.02 g or gyro bias > 0.5°/s triggers re-calibration.
Step 1: Daily static. Save session file with timestamp and metadata: device_id, firmware, temp_C, operator. Compute bias_today = df_static.mean() and noise_today = df_static.std().
Step 2: Compute RMSE vs baseline: rmse = sqrt(mean((bias_today - bias_baseline)**2)). Log rmse and append to camp_timeseries.csv.
Step 3: Plot trends. Create a daily plot of bias and RMSE. If slope of bias vs day > threshold, inspect sensor housing and connectors.
Step 4: Action rules. If rmse_accel > 0.02 g or rmse_gyro > 0.5°/s, re-run full calibration and mark sessions since last good calibration as suspect.
Step 5: Document fixes. When re-calibrating, save new calibration file with notes and link to affected session IDs. Notify coach with short status: 'Sensor X re-calibrated; sessions 3–5 flagged'.
Kort sagt: do daily static tests, log, compute RMSE, and act when thresholds exceeded. Keep it simple and automated.

task_instruction: Compose a brief guide for building a reproducible field-to-analysis pipeline with metadata capture.
task_details: Audience: analysts and data managers. Include required metadata (device ID, firmware, calibration, sampling rates, operator, location), data storage tips (parquet, timezones), version control (git for code, data hashes), and simple commands like df.to_parquet and git commit. Provide stepwise imperatives and a TL;DR.
personalized:
TL;DR: capture metadata at collection, store raw files and calibration alongside, use versioned scripts and compressed columnar files (parquet). Kort sagt: metadata saves hours later.
Problem: missing context (which device, which calibration) makes post-hoc analysis unreliable. Løsning: standardize a small metadata JSON saved with each session and use reproducible scripts to process raw -> cleaned -> features.
Praktisk anbefaling: always save session_meta.json with device_id, fw_version, calibration_file, sampling_rates, operator, timezone, and GPS start coord. Use df.to_parquet('session.parquet', compression='snappy').
Step 1: Capture metadata. Create session_meta = {'session_id':..., 'device_id':..., 'calibration': 'cal_20260101.json', 'fs': {'gps':1,'imu':100}, 'operator':'name', 'location':'Østmarka', 'tz':'Europe/Oslo'} and write to disk.
Step 2: Store raw and processed separately. Raw/ contains original logs; proc/ contains cleaned parquet and feature tables. Use consistent filenames like YYYYMMDD_athlete_session.parquet.
Step 3: Version code. Put processing scripts and notebooks under git. Commit changes and tag releases: git tag v1.0_analysis.
Step 4: Data integrity. Compute and store file hashes for raw files (sha256) so you can verify later.
Step 5: Reproducible run. Create a small run script that accepts session_id and writes outputs to proc/ with metadata on software versions. Example: python process.py --session session123.
Kort sagt: collect metadata, separate raw/proc, version code, and hash raw files. Do this once and your camp analyses will be traceable and faster.

personalized: Release: XC-Ski-SensorSet v1.0. What: 120 anonymized training runs with GPS/IMU (100 Hz/10 Hz), HR and cadence metadata, and a data dictionary. Format: CSV per-run, segment JSON, and example TFRecord for ML. Download: DOI 10.0000/xc-ski.1 or https://github.com/ORG/xc-ski-sensors (LFS). Privacy: all personal identifiers removed, consent obtained for research use only. Cite: use the included citation.bib. Quick load: import pandas as pd; run = pd.read_csv('run_001_gps.csv'). Limitations: uneven sampling in a few runs and sensor clock drift up to 2s—see notes. Contribute: upload additional runs via the contributor workflow on GitHub, include sensor spec and consent statement. PRs welcome for data loaders and validators. Kort sagt: use for method development, report anomalies, and contribute more runs if you have consent.

task_instruction: Publish a patch release note explaining a bugfix and upgrade steps.
task_details: Compose a concise patch release announcement (v1.0.1) that fixes a smoothing/Kalman filter bug affecting vertical speed estimates. Include what changed, why it matters (RMSE improvement), how to upgrade with pip, migration notes (no API change), test coverage details, and where to report regressions. Keep pragmatic tone and include a quick test command to confirm fix.
personalized: Release: skiski-analysis v1.0.1. What: fixes a Kalman-filter bug that biased vertical speed and elevation-derived power. Why it matters: vertical speed RMSE reduced from 0.35 m/s to 0.18 m/s on our validation set. How to upgrade: pip install --upgrade skiski-analysis==1.0.1. Migration: no API changes; existing scripts should run unchanged. Verify: run python -m skiski.tests.test_altitude_fix to run the regression check. Tests: added unit tests and a small integration test against recorded sensor streams. Report: open an issue if you see new regressions or changed behaviour. Practical recommendation: reprocess any saved elevation-derived metrics if accuracy matters. PRs welcome for further validation scripts.

personalized: Release: sensor-examples sprint. What: we need practical sensor integration examples for MPU9250, ICM-20948 and common GPS modules, plus Arduino/ESP32 code for real-time logging. persona.interests_lifestyle: cross-country and backcountry skiing, weekend training camps and local races, cycling and trail running in summer, building open-source data visualization tools, tinkering with sensors and Arduino/IMU prototypes, reading sports science journals, coaching youth skiing, Strava and GPS route analysis, sauna and coffee culture, travel to World Cup events, photography of training environments

general_writing_style.syntax: Favors short-to-medium sentences in active voice and uses imperatives for recommendations (e.g., "Validate this sensor", "Reduce smoothing"). general_writing_style.lexicon: Mixes sports-science and data-analytic vocabulary: GPS, IMU, cadence, vertical speed, VO2max, lactate threshold, watts, W/kg, RMSE, smoothing, Kalman filter, Python/R/SQL. general_writing_style.linguistic_patterns: Frequently uses slashes and acronyms ("GPS/IMU", "HR/power/pace") and short pragmatic markers to signal summaries or actions: "Kort sagt:", "Praktisk anbefaling:", "TL;DR:". task_instruction: Research partnership pitch offering team data for a peer-reviewed study.
